title: Lumos: Human-First WebMCP for Transparent AI Collaboration
pitch: Lumos lets people and AI agents collaborate through explicit consent, scoped tools, clear action previews, and user-controlled execution—built on WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Lumos lets people and AI agents collaborate through explicit consent, scoped tools, clear action previews, and user-controlled execution—built on WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates For WebMCP Challenge judges Live URL: https://welockai.com/panel/ Repository: https://github.com/candasoz01-cmd/lumos-core License: Apache-2.0 Open in: ChatGPT’s in-app browser, or Google Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Lumos exposes three task-board tools through document.modelContext : lumos-list-tasks , lumos-propose-task , and lumos-complete-task . Reading requires explicit session-scoped sharing consent. Every write is previewed and confirmed inside Lumos. Declining writes nothing, and completing a task cannot be used to discover task existence without consent. The recorded native proof used Chrome 152. ChatGPT’s in-app browser was not used as the recorded native proof; the live Lumos panel is the judge-facing surface. Inspiration AI agents can move quickly through software, but speed without visible authority boundaries can undermine trust. Lumos already had a task board and a human approval flow. For the WebMCP Challenge, we explored a focused question: how can an agent use a real product surface without taking the final decision away from the person? What it does Lumos exposes three task-board tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() : lumos-list-tasks reads the task board only after the user explicitly approves sharing it with agents. The permission is session-scoped, visible in the panel, and revocable. lumos-propose-task proposes a task but does not create it until the user approves the panel's own confirmation dialog. lumos-complete-task requires board-sharing consent first, then a separate approval before changing a task's status. The confirmation preview shows the exact fields involved, including title, priority, schedule, status, source, and status transition. Cancelling produces no write. If WebMCP is unavailable, Lumos fails closed, registers no tools, marks the surface unsupported, and continues as a normal panel without a shim or polyfill. How we built it The public Lumos panel is built with Astro and browser-native JavaScript. A narrow bridge in the existing panel runtime connects WebMCP tools to the established task workflow. The tools return MCP-compatible content payloads and reuse the same task persistence and confirmation paths as the human-facing interface. The implementation includes source-contract tests and a Playwright end-to-end harness that exercises tool registration, consent refusal, approval, cancellation, task creation, and completion. The harness simulates the browser's agent-side WebMCP host so it validates the page implementation without pretending to be native browser proof. The public panel is deployed on Vercel, and the source is available under the Apache-2.0 license. What changed during the challenge Lumos, its panel, task module, and approval flow existed before August 25, 2026. The WebMCP-specific layer was added during the challenge period. That work added the three tool registrations, session-scoped read consent, per-mutation approval, full-field action previews, fail-closed behavior, and automated verification. Security review also led to concrete fixes: task data is no longer returned without sharing consent; task-completion lookups cannot reveal whether a task exists before consent; and a stale dialog-close event can no longer cancel a later approval prompt. Challenges we faced The hardest part was treating privacy and consent as implementation details rather than slogans. A read-only task list can still contain sensitive personal or work information. A confirmation that hides priority or schedule is not meaningful consent. Different error responses can also leak whether a task exists. WebMCP is emerging, so we also had to keep three kinds of evidence separate: source behavior, harness-based end-to-end verification, and native browser-agent invocation. Lumos does not add a compatibility shim when the platform API is missing. What we learned Read-only does not automatically mean safe to share. Approval must show every field that will be written. Refusal and failure need different machine-readable results. Unsupported environments should fail closed without changing the ordinary product. Human control works best when it is part of the product flow, not an agent-side promise. What's next Next we will expand native live-origin verification as supporting browsers expose WebMCP, preserve raw evidence for agent discovery and invocation, and continue testing consent revocation and approval behavior across clients. The goal remains the same: useful agent collaboration with authority, privacy, and final control kept visibly in human hands.
